title: Delegated Attestation Ledger & Evidence TTL — Pricing Pilot
creator: Avery Patel
description:
Summary:
This pilot introduces a lightweight cryptographically-backed evidence ledger for customer security attestations and a configurable evidence TTL (time-to-live) model. It pairs a delegated attestation flow (where customers can sign, delegate, and periodically refresh claims) with a pricing experiment that tests per-evidence credits vs. a subscription bundle for high-volume enterprise customers.

Problem:
Enterprise contracts and SIG/CAIQ responses drive a disproportionate amount of sales friction and manual effort from solutions and legal teams. Customers repeatedly request the same pieces of evidence; internal ops ends up reproducing answers and pushing signed artifacts repeatedly. Current attestation handling lacks an auditable ledger and has no concept of evidence currency or expiration, which increases support load and creates ambiguity for pricing.

Hypothesis:
If we provide a verifiable evidence ledger + configurable TTL and a pricing option aligned to evidence churn, then customers will self-serve more attestations (reducing sales/SE workload) and we will capture incremental revenue from high-frequency attestation consumers while maintaining conversion for low-volume customers.

Proposed solution (high level):
1) Evidence ledger: store immutable ledger entries for attestations (signed metadata, issuer, dates, references to CAIQ sections). Each ledger entry emits a short verifiable token (signed JSON Web Token) that customers can include with RFPs. Ledger entries are searchable in the Console and exportable to audit logs.
2) Delegated attestations: support an optional delegated signature flow where customer contacts (or third-party auditors) can attach a verified claim to a ledger entry. Delegation is captured with provenance metadata and opt-in sharing controls.
3) Evidence TTL: allow admins to set TTLs per evidence type (e.g., pen-test report 12 months, architecture diagram 6 months). After TTL expiry evidence is flagged as stale, and the Console surfaces a one-click refresh flow with recommended scope changes.
4) Pricing experiment: two cohorts — (A) per-evidence credit model (pay per refresh or new ledger entry) with bundled free credits for new accounts; (B) subscription model for heavy users (monthly allotment of refreshes + priority handling). Control cohort sees current manual-handling process but with new UI visibility.

Instrumentation and success metrics:
- Primary metrics: self-serve attestation uptake (target 25% of pilot customers), average time to complete security questionnaire (target -30% vs baseline), support tickets citing evidence requests (target -40%), ARR from subscription cohort (target > $X/month after 3 months).
- Secondary metrics: number of ledger entries per customer, average TTL expiry rate, conversion lift for enterprise contracts where attestation bundle was required.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: Console UI for ledger + refresh flow, backend ledger API, signed tokens, basic delegated-signing UI, pricing hooks and billing integration for credit/subscription usage, dashboards for metrics.
- Non-goals: full PKI/HSM-hosted signing or complex legal workflows for delegated third-party attestations (we will stub full legal integrations for pilot).

Rollout plan:
- Week 1: Finalize PRD and API schema, engineering spike for signed tokens and TTL enforcement.
- Week 2: Build Console ledger UI, refresh flow, and basic delegated-signing modal; integrate billing hooks.
- Week 3: Internal dogfooding with Solutions/SE; design review and copy improvements.
- Week 4: Launch closed beta to 8 selected enterprise customers segmented by attestation volume; A/B split into pricing cohorts.
- 60-day evaluation: measure metrics and iterate on pricing; prepare a decision for expansion or rollback.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Customers treat TTL as prescriptive and request legal re-tests more frequently. Mitigation: communicate recommended TTLs as guidance and include clear opt-in revalidation steps; add support SLA for paid bundles.
- Risk: Billing disputes due to unexpected charges for refreshes. Mitigation: surface upcoming TTL expiries and preview estimated charges before refresh is executed; include free grace credit per quarter in subscription plan.
- Risk: Delegated signatures increase legal surface. Mitigation: restrict delegated flow to metadata-level attestations in pilot and capture audit logs for all signings.

Open questions:
- Should TTL defaults be conservative (longer) or aggressive (shorter) to drive refresh revenue?
- What is the minimum free-credit allocation that balances conversion with cost?
- Do we require customer-signed acceptance of billing terms on first refresh?

Next steps:
- Approvals: product + security + billing + legal alignment (security review requested).
- Engineering spike ticket: ENG-703211 (ledger POC with signed tokens).
- Design tasks: DES-703212 (Console UI + refresh modal).
- Set up measurement dashboard (analytics owner: Growth).
acceptance_criteria:
1) Console shows ledger entries with signed tokens and TTL status for pilot customers.
2) Delegated signing modal allows attaching provenance metadata and records audit trail.
3) Billing records reflect credit consumption and subscription allotments; preview shown before charge.
4) Closed beta to 8 customers started; instrumentation captures self-serve uptake, time-to-complete, support ticket delta, and revenue.
5) Post-60-day decision ready with clear go/no-go recommendation and next-step pricing proposal.
decisions:
- Use signed JWT tokens for verifiable ledger artifacts (accepted 2025-02-14).
- Pilot will limit delegated attestations to metadata-level signatures (no third-party legal integrations yet).
- Two-cohort pricing experiment chosen to compare per-evidence vs subscription lanes.
- Default TTLs will be conservative for beta (longer durations) to avoid customer churn; iterate after metric review.
